newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-S-E-Banken profit could lure partners.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S-E-Banken profit could lure partners.

text.p: Swedish high street bank S-E-Banken on Friday posted a better than expected 68 percent leap in 1996 profits which analysts said could help the bank find a partner for expansion.

The banking arm of the Wallenberg industrial empire, which has been actively seeking to expand in recent months, posted an operating profit of 5.87 billion crowns ($792 million), a record in its 25 year history, and above expectations of 5.68 billion crowns.
Loan losses slumped 66 percent to 1.11 billion crowns, corresponding to 0.52 percent of the total loan portfolio compared with 1.56 percent in 1995.

"A sparkling performance was reported by the bank in the fourth quarter," Paribas bank analyst Peter Thorn said. "This could help the share price and the bank may even find it easier to renegotiate a merger in Sweden."
S-E-Banken shares were 1.5 crowns higher at 72 crowns in heavy trading on Friday afternoon.
S-E-Banken has been on the prowl for growth since Sweden's bank sector recovered from a rocky period in the early 1990s.

Last September it was reported to be interested in merging with another of Sweden's big four banks, Handelsbanken. But this bit the dust when Handelsbanken made a cash takeover bid for mortgage bank Stadshypotek.
Rumours of a marriage of S-E-Banken and state-controlled bank Nordbanken emerged late last year.
But this plan also hit a dead-end earlier this month with the two banks saying talks had ended without conclusion. No further details were given on the breakdown in merger talks.
Analysts expected S-E-Banken to continue looking to expand and saw another Swedish bank or insurer as the most likely fit.

S-E-Banken, attributing its high profit to falling interest rates, declining lending losses and growing volumes in important areas, said it wanted to strengthen its position through clearly target-oriented work.
It posted a four percent rise in 1996 income to 17.81 billion crowns, saying return on equity rose to 22.7 percent against 10.7 percent.
Earnings per share rose to 8.91 crowns from 4.80 crowns and the bank proposed a dividend payment of 2.75 crowns a share compared with 1.50 crowns in 1995.

Chief executive Bjorn Svedberg said the bank was now financially strong and ready for growth. A Nordic expansion had been successful in Norway and Finland, and the bank was further strengthened this year by setting up a Danish branch.
"We now have a firm basis to act from in the future," Svedberg said in a statement.

"Our main strategy is to continue investing in our core products in the Nordic region and internationally. Our focus on strong customer segments is supported by sophisticated IT-systems to further advance our leading position."
Analyst Olaf Conrad from Morgan Stanley said the 1996 result was very positive for S-E-Banken but did not necessarily mean other Swedish banks would be so strong.
"S-E-Banken has benefited from favourable developments in the capital markets," Conrad told Reuters.
"I would not expect to see similar net interest income from any other of the banks because they are much less aggressive than S-E-banken in riding the yield curve."
Handelsbanken and Nordbanken are due to release 1996 reports on February 18 and Swedbank on February 19.
